papers.version_note: The text is a saved web page of a vendor lesson (site navigation first, then the lesson, then a link list). The text layer has no page breaks, so it is treated as one page. Some inline citations lost their subject in the text layer (for example the sentence on power consumption starts with the bare reference number 7).
papers.what_it_is: A vendor primer from Quantum Computing Inc that explains what a qudit is, how superposition and interference are used, and how qudits are used in its feedback-based entropy quantum computing (EQC) analog optimizer.

assertions.value: The authors state that entropy quantum computing (EQC) is a paradigm for optimization that uses quantum optics and nanophotonics.
assertions.anchor: Introduction to Qudits in EQC, first paragraph
quotes: Entropy quantum computing (EQC) is a unique paradigm for optimization using quantum optics and nanophotonics.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own paradigm; the lesson gives no technical detail of it.

assertions.value: The authors state that most quantum and quantum-inspired programming models use qubits, and that even quantum annealing models are restricted to qubits, while EQC can use qudits.
assertions.anchor: Introduction to Qudits in EQC, first paragraph
quotes: Most quantum and quantum-inspired programming models use qubits, even quantum annealing models are restricted to qubits.
EQC has the ability to use qudits
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's general statement about other models, with no citation in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors define qudits as units of quantum information that take more than two possible states.
assertions.anchor: Introduction to Qudits in EQC, first paragraph
quotes: qudits, which are units of quantum information taking more than 2 possible states
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the definition of a qudit in its first paragraph.

assertions.value: The authors state that superposition makes qubits powerful, and that combining superposition with the ability to represent more than two levels makes computing with qudits powerful. The lesson gives no proof or measurement for this.
assertions.anchor: Introduction to Qudits in EQC, first paragraph
quotes: The property of quantum mechanics known as superposition is what makes qubits powerful. Combining superposition and the ability to represent more than 2 levels makes computing with qudits so powerful.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson states no complexity or performance advantage of qudits over qubits.

assertions.value: The authors state that qudits can be used in digital quantum computing or in analog computing.
assertions.anchor: Introduction to Qudits in EQC, first paragraph
quotes: Qudits can be used in digital quantum computing or analog computing .
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without a citation or evidence in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state the scope of the lesson: it explains what a qudit is with respect to feedback-based EQC, which it calls an analog paradigm rather than digital quantum gates, and which manipulates qudit states to minimize an objective function. The lesson does not give the details of EQC.
assertions.anchor: Introduction to Qudits in EQC, first paragraph
quotes: Without getting into the details of EQC in this document, we will discuss what a qudit is with respect to its implementation in feedback-based EQC (an analog paradigm, rather than digital quantum gates), which manipulates qudit states to minimize an objective function.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states its own scope in the first section.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson has no experiment, no data and no hardware specification; it is a conceptual primer.

assertions.value: The authors state that a qudit can be constrained mathematically to behave like a qubit. They give the reason that the equation X squared equals X holds only for X equal to 0 or 1, and not for X greater than 1.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, second paragraph
quotes: We first note that mathematically a qudit can be constrained to behave like a qubit.
X 2 = X X^2=X X 2 = X is only satisfied if X = 0 X=0 X = 0 or X = 1 X=1 X = 1 , but not for X > 1 X>1 X > 1
assertions.certainty_reason: A short argument in a vendor primer, not a stated theorem with conditions; the arithmetic fact is elementary for integer-valued X.
assertions.reader_inference: The fact holds for real X only at 0 and 1; the lesson does not say which domain X is taken from.

assertions.value: The authors state that adding a penalty term, the square of (X squared minus X), weighted by a lambda that is large and positive, forces a qudit system to behave like a binary model, which they call the NP-hard quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) setting.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, second paragraph
quotes: Therefore by adding a term λ ( X 2 − X ) 2
is large and positive, we can force a qudit system to behave like a perhaps more familiar binary model, the familiar (and NP-hard) quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) setting.
assertions.certainty_reason: A sketched penalty construction in a vendor primer, without a stated bound on lambda or a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the standard penalty-method idea; the lesson does not say how large lambda must be.

assertions.value: The authors state that in practice a slightly different approach than the penalty term works better for their hardware, and they do not describe that approach.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, second paragraph
quotes: We find that in practice a slightly different approach works better for our hardware
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor statement about its own hardware, with no data in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: No comparison between the two approaches is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that anything which can be expressed in terms of qubits can also be expressed in terms of qudits.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, second paragraph
quotes: anything which can be expressed in terms of qubits can also be expressed in terms of qudits
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim supported only by the penalty-term sketch in the same section.

assertions.value: The authors state that many real-world problems are naturally integer rather than binary. They give production planning with integer product quantities and finance with an integer number of shares as examples.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, third paragraph
quotes: many real-world problems are naturally integer rather than binary
integer problems arise in production planning where products can only be made in integer quantities
Integer problems can similarly arise in finance, if only an integer number of shares can be purchased.
assertions.certainty_reason: General examples given by the authors, with no data.

assertions.value: The authors state that qudits which can take many values can be used to approximate continuous variables. They give how full to fill a fuel tank, to balance loss of efficiency due to weight against more frequent stops, as an example of a continuous problem variable.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, third paragraph
quotes: qudits which can take many values can be used to approximate continuous variables
how full to fill a fuel tank on a machine to balance loss of efficiency due to weight against having to stop more frequently to refill
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with an illustrative example and no error analysis.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson gives no bound on the approximation error as a function of the number of levels.

assertions.value: The authors state that their qudit-based paradigm allows them to work in a traditional binary setting or to explore integer models, and to some extent continuous models.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, last sentence
quotes: Our qudit-based paradigm allows the flexibility to both work in a traditional binary setting or to explore what can be done with integer (and too some extent continuous) models
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes the flexibility of its own paradigm.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike bits in a conventional computer, qubits and qudits take on multiple values at the same time, which they call superposition, and that during computation each qudit takes on multiple values at the same time, enabling greater exploration of a problem search space.
quotes: Unlike information encoded using bits in a conventional computer, qubits and qudits take on multiple values at the same time. This is called superpostion.
each qudit will take on multiple values at the same time, enabling greater exploration of a problem search space
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines superposition in its own words in the Superposition section.
assertions.reader_inference: The phrase 'multiple values at the same time' is a popular simplification; a superposition is a weighted sum of basis states with amplitudes.

assertions.value: The authors describe a quantum die as an example of a qudit: for a six-sided die, the superposition of states is a sum of amplitudes alpha one to alpha six, each multiplying the ket of one face.
quotes: think of a quantum die. Six sides, for common dice the superposition of states would be described by:
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson writes the state of its quantum die example in the Superposition section.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson does not state the normalization condition on the amplitudes.

assertions.value: The authors give a worked example: the quadratic function f(x) minus two x one squared minus two x two squared plus x one times x two, over a domain from 0 to 99 for each variable, has two solutions at the same minimum value under the constraint that x one plus x two equals 99. The solutions [99, 0] and [0,99] give f equal to minus 19602.
quotes: has two solutions at the same minimum value under the constraint x 1 + x 2 = 99
These solutions ` [99, 0] ` and ` [0,99] ` result in f ( x ) = − 19602
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked arithmetic example given by the authors in a vendor primer; it is not run on hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: Checked by hand: on the constraint the function equals minus 19602 plus five times x one times x two, so the minimum is at the two end points, as stated. The lesson does not say which of two readings of the sentence 'minimum value' it uses (over the constraint line), but this reading is the one that fits.

assertions.value: The authors state that the example states are potentially evaluated at the same time in superposition, so that when a state is read multiple times from the system, both solutions should appear with the same frequency, and that other states such as [1, 98], [98, 1], [49, 50] and [50, 49] also exist in the superposition.
quotes: are potentially evaluated at the same time, so when a state is read multiple times from the system, both solutions should appear with the same frequency
Not only do these states exist in superposition, but also ` [1, 98] `, ` [98, 1] `, ` [49, 50] `, ` [50, 49] `, and so on.
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative statement by the authors; no device run is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: This describes an unbiased superposition; the lesson does not say that the device prepares it.

assertions.value: The authors state that superposition by itself is not useful for optimization: if measured, any of the answers would be equally likely, so the device would effectively be a random number generator, which they call another of their products.
quotes: By itself this superposition isn't actually useful for optimization, if we measured it we would be equally likely to measure any of the answers it would effectively be a random number generator (another one of our products).
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that to use a device as a quantum optimizer, the potential solutions must be interfered so that less optimal solutions cancel out and more optimal solutions reinforce, and that using interference is at the heart of all quantum optimisation techniques.
quotes: we need to interfere these potential solutions in such a way that less optimal solutions cancel out, and more optimal solutions reinforce
Using interference in a clever way to get good solutions is at the heart of all quantum optimisation techniques
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement by the authors without proof or citation in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that optical techniques have the advantage that they can also take advantage of non-linear optical effects, for example to amplify signals.
quotes: optical techniques have the advantage that they can also take advantage of non-linear optical effects, for example, to amplify signals
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes the advantage of its own technology class; no data is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that, depending on the device, sub-optimal solutions may appear with various frequency; that a solution state is read with a certain probability; and that crafting an objective function is about increasing the likelihood that a desirable state is read.
quotes: Depending on the device, sub-optimal solutions may appear with various frequency.
A solution state is read from the device with a certain probability and crafting an objective function is about increasing the likelyhood that a desireable state is read.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state in the Superposition section that the readout of the device is probabilistic and can return sub-optimal solutions.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson does not report how often sub-optimal solutions appear on any device.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum superposition is different from and more powerful than standard classical probability distributions, because classical probabilities can only add while quantum amplitudes can add or subtract, and that this ability to subtract is the interference phenomenon.
quotes: Quantum superposition, explained conceptually in [ 6 ], is different from and more powerful than standard classical probability distributions
while classical probabilities can only add, quantum amplitudes can add or subtract. This ability to subtract is the interference phenomena
assertions.certainty_reason: A conceptual explanation that the authors cite to another source; no proof in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement is a standard textbook point; 'more powerful' is not defined in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum superpositions are fragile and can be destroyed by measurement, which converts them into ordinary probability distributions, so quantum devices and algorithms need to be designed to preserve the superpositions until the result is read out.
quotes: Quantum superpositions are fragile, and can be destroyed by measurement, which converts them into ordinary probability distributions.
quantum devices and algorithms need to be designed carefully in a way which preserves these superpositions until the result is read out
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of quantum superposition in the Superposition section.

assertions.value: The authors state that feedback-based EQC is an analog system. In an analog computer, a physical model represents a mathematical one through the initialization of physical states, the physical system evolves until a stopping condition is reached, and the measurements are then translated into values in the domain of the mathematical model.
quotes: Feedback-based EQC is an analog system, which defines how a qudit is leveraged to perform computation.
This physical system evolves until a stopping condition is reached, then the measurements of the system are translated into values in the domain of the mathematical model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines its analog computing model in the Analog System section.

assertions.value: The authors state that one of the most attractive benefits of analog computing at nanoscale is low power consumption. They state that cited devices consume power during operation on the order of a Mac Pro at idle, about 50W. The text layer lost the name of the devices, so the subject of the sentence is missing.
quotes: One of the most attractive benefits of analog computing at nanoscale is the miserly power consumption.
consume power during operation on the order of the consumption of a Mac Pro at idle (~50W)[ 8 ].
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor power figure that rests on two citations (reference 7 for the devices, reference 8 for the Mac Pro figure) and is not measured in the lesson; the subject is lost in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence has no stated device, so the figure cannot be tied to the Dirac-1 or any other product from this text alone. The link list names the Dirac-1 Technical Brief, which may be reference 7.

assertions.value: The authors state that a critical aspect of computing with qudits on analog devices is the translation of the measurements to the domain of the problem, which they call decoding. Measurements may be discrete, such as counting photon arrivals, or continuous, such as recording volumes of fluid.
quotes: is the translation of the measurements to the domain of the problem. This can be referred to as "decoding".
discrete measurements could be counting events such as photon arrivals and continuous measurements could be recording volumes of fluid
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines decoding in the Computation section.

assertions.value: The authors state that counts of photons in certain modes are translated to a mathematical model by relative intensity or a binary response; that unless the mathematical model has a 1-to-1 mapping with the photon counts, the meaning in the solution will likely be in a continuous domain; and that approximation methods can be used to convert between continuous and discrete or vice versa.
quotes: counts of photons in certain modes are translated to a mathematical model by relative intensity or a binary response
unless the mathematical model has a 1-to-1 mapping with the photon counts, the meaning in the solution will likely be in a continuous domain
approximation methods can be used to convert between continuous and discrete or vice versa
assertions.certainty_reason: A description by the authors without a worked decoding or data.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson does not say which decoding Dirac-1 uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that n qudits with dimensionality k translate to a solution vector of size n, with each element having k possible values, and that the number of variables is the most common measure of the size of a model.
quotes: The most common measure of the size of a model is the number of variables
n n n qudits with dimensionality k k k will translate to a solution vector of size n n n , with each element having k k k possible values
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines the relation between qudit count, dimensionality and solution vector in the Qudit Dimensionality section.

assertions.value: The authors state that when taking l samples to test the effect of superposition, fewer than l distinct vectors will be produced, and each vector will appear fewer than l times. The lesson gives no measured sample.
quotes: When taking l l l samples to test the effect of superposition, m < l m<l m < l distinct vectors will be produced
assertions.certainty_reason: A generic statement by the authors without an experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: As written, the statement that fewer than l distinct vectors always appear is not guaranteed for any finite l; it holds only when some vector repeats. The lesson gives no condition.

assertions.value: The authors state in the conclusion that the primer has described what qudits are in relation to EQC, the power made possible through superposition, their use in analog computation, and the translation between a physical system and a mathematical model.
quotes: This primer on qudits has described what qudits are in relation to EQC, the power made possible through superposition, their use in analog computation and translation between a physical system and a mathematical model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The conclusion states the scope of the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson contains no experimental result, benchmark or hardware figure of merit.
